Employee Turnover Analytics

A Guided Machine Learning Analysis for Portobello Tech

Analyst: David Farmer
Project type: Classification, clustering, and employee-retention analysis
Dataset: HR_comma_sep.csv
Target: left — 0 = stayed, 1 = left

How to use this notebook¶

This notebook follows the problem statement in the same numbered order. Every assignment question has three blocks:

  1. Question block — what the assignment asks and what the output should show.
  2. Work block — the code cell where the analysis will be written.
  3. Interpretation checkpoint — the explanation that turns an output into an answer.

Work from top to bottom. Complete and verify one numbered question before moving to the next. The notebook intentionally provides structure and prompts rather than finished solutions.

Interpretation checkpoint — Question 1¶

  • How many missing values were found?
  • Were duplicate rows found, and how will they be handled?
  • Do the data types match the meaning of each column?
  • Are the observed numeric ranges plausible?

Write the conclusion here:

The dataset contains no missing values, with a missing-value percentage of 0% for every feature. However, 3,008 exact matching rows were identified. Because the dataset does not include a unique employee identifier, it is not possible to determine whether these rows are accidental duplicates or different employees who share the same recorded characteristics. Therefore, the matching rows will be retained during the exploratory data analysis and reconsidered before model training. The observed numeric ranges are plausible: satisfaction_level ranges from 0.09 to 1.00, while last_evaluation ranges from 0.36 to 1.00. Both variables remain within their expected 0-to-1 boundaries, and no invalid values were identified.

# Create a separate DataFrame for the joint workload analysis
workload_analysis = df[
    [
        "number_project",
        "average_montly_hours",
        "time_spend_company",
        "last_evaluation",
        "left"
    ]
].copy()

# Group average monthly hours into interpretable ranges
workload_analysis["hours_group"] = pd.cut(
    workload_analysis["average_montly_hours"],
    bins=[0, 150, 200, 250, float("inf")],
    labels=[
        "150 or less",
        "151–200",
        "201–250",
        "More than 250"
    ],
    include_lowest=True
)

# Group employee tenure into interpretable ranges
workload_analysis["tenure_group"] = pd.cut(
    workload_analysis["time_spend_company"],
    bins=[0, 2, 3, 4, 5, float("inf")],
    labels=[
        "2 years",
        "3 years",
        "4 years",
        "5 years",
        "6+ years"
    ],
    include_lowest=True
)

# Group evaluation scores into low, moderate, and high categories
workload_analysis["evaluation_group"] = pd.cut(
    workload_analysis["last_evaluation"],
    bins=[0, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00],
    labels=[
        "Low (0.50 or less)",
        "Moderate (0.51–0.75)",
        "High (above 0.75)"
    ],
    include_lowest=True
)

# Preserve the intended category order
tenure_groups = workload_analysis[
    "tenure_group"
].cat.categories

evaluation_groups = workload_analysis[
    "evaluation_group"
].cat.categories

# Produce one figure for each evaluation group
for evaluation in evaluation_groups:

    evaluation_data = workload_analysis[
        workload_analysis["evaluation_group"] == evaluation
    ]

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(
        2,
        3,
        figsize=(18, 11)
    )

    axes = axes.flatten()

    # Produce one panel for each tenure group
    for panel_index, (ax, tenure) in enumerate(
        zip(axes, tenure_groups)
    ):

        panel_data = evaluation_data[
            evaluation_data["tenure_group"] == tenure
        ]

        # Calculate the turnover rate for each
        # project-count and monthly-hours combination
        turnover_rates = panel_data.pivot_table(
            index="number_project",
            columns="hours_group",
            values="left",
            aggfunc="mean",
            observed=False
        ) * 100

        # Count employees in each combination
        observation_counts = panel_data.pivot_table(
            index="number_project",
            columns="hours_group",
            values="left",
            aggfunc="size",
            observed=False
        )

        # Hide combinations containing fewer than 20 employees
        low_sample_mask = observation_counts < 20

        sns.heatmap(
            turnover_rates,
            mask=low_sample_mask,
            annot=True,
            fmt=".1f",
            cmap="YlOrRd",
            vmin=0,
            vmax=100,
            linewidths=0.5,
            cbar=(panel_index == 0),
            cbar_kws={"label": "Turnover rate (%)"},
            ax=ax
        )

        ax.set_title(f"Tenure: {tenure}")
        ax.set_xlabel("Average monthly hours")
        ax.set_ylabel("Number of projects")

    # Remove the unused sixth panel
    for unused_ax in axes[len(tenure_groups):]:
        unused_ax.remove()

    fig.suptitle(
        (
            "Turnover Rate by Projects, Monthly Hours, and Tenure\n"
            f"Last Evaluation: {evaluation}"
        ),
        fontsize=16,
        y=1.02
    )

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

Interpretation checkpoint — Question 2.1¶

  • Which numerical features have the strongest correlations with left?
  • Are those correlations weak, moderate, or strong?
  • Which relationships deserve closer visual investigation?

Write the inference here:

time spent at the company has the strongest positive correlation with turnover relative to the other features, but it is still only a weak relationship in absolute terms. High-performing employees exposed to sustained heavy workloads—particularly high monthly hours and numerous projects after several years with the company—show a substantially elevated turnover rate. The correlation analysis shows that no single workload or tenure feature has a strong linear relationship with employee turnover. However, the joint analysis reveals important nonlinear patterns that are not visible in the pairwise correlation matrix. Employees with low or moderate evaluations, three years of tenure, two projects, and fewer than 200 monthly hours show high turnover rates, suggesting a potentially underutilized or disengaged employee profile. A second profile appears among highly evaluated employees with four or more years of tenure who are assigned numerous projects and work more than 200 hours per month. Turnover generally increases as both project count and monthly hours rise within this group, suggesting a possible overwork or burnout risk. These explanations cannot be confirmed from the available data, but the observed patterns indicate that employee turnover may depend more on interactions among evaluation, workload, and tenure than on any single feature independently. These relationships should be examined further during predictive modeling.

Interpretation checkpoint — Question 2.2¶

  • Is each distribution symmetric, skewed, multimodal, or clustered?
  • Where do employees who left appear concentrated?
  • What possible workload or satisfaction patterns should be tested later?

Write the inference here:

The distributions reveal several distinct employee-turnover profiles. Satisfaction among employees who stayed is broadly concentrated at moderate-to-high levels, with relatively few employees at very low satisfaction. In contrast, the satisfaction distribution for employees who left is multimodal, with noticeable concentrations near very low satisfaction, around 0.40, and again at higher satisfaction levels. This suggests that turnover is not limited to dissatisfied employees and may occur for different reasons among different employee groups.

The last-evaluation distribution for employees who stayed is broad and relatively balanced rather than strongly skewed. Employees who left show a distinctly bimodal distribution, with one cluster around evaluation scores of 0.50 and another among highly evaluated employees near 0.85–1.00. Average monthly hours show a similar pattern: employees who stayed are distributed broadly around the middle of the range, while employees who left are concentrated in two groups—approximately 130–160 hours and 240–300 hours per month.

Together, these distributions suggest two possible turnover profiles: employees with lower satisfaction, lower evaluations, and comparatively low monthly hours may be underutilized or disengaged, while highly evaluated employees working substantially more hours may be experiencing excessive workload or burnout. These explanations remain hypotheses, but later modeling should test whether satisfaction, evaluation, and monthly hours interact to predict turnover more effectively than any individual feature alone.

The bimodal patterns in the distribution plots are consistent with the two turnover profiles. The joint heatmaps indicated elevated turnover among relatively underloaded employees and among highly evaluated employees experiencing heavier workloads. These distribution plots confirmed that employees who left were concentrated near both the lower and upper ends of evaluation scores and monthly working hours.

2.3 Draw the Employee Project-Count Bar Plot for Employees Who Left and Stayed¶

Use number_project on the horizontal axis and left as the hue.

In [9]:
# TODO 2.3: Plot project counts for employees who stayed and left.
# Sanity check: compare raw counts carefully because the two target classes are imbalanced.

# Define the project-count order
project_order = sorted(df["number_project"].unique())

# Calculate raw counts by project count and turnover status
project_counts = pd.crosstab(
    df["number_project"],
    df["left"]
).reindex(
    index=project_order,
    columns=[0, 1],
    fill_value=0
)

# Calculate percentages within each project-count group
project_percentages = (
    project_counts.div(project_counts.sum(axis=1), axis=0) * 100
)

# Draw the grouped bar plot
plt.figure(figsize=(11, 6))

ax = sns.countplot(
    data=df,
    x="number_project",
    hue="left",
    order=project_order,
    hue_order=[0, 1],
    palette={
        0: "#9AA0A6",  # Stayed
        1: "#D62728"   # Left
    }
)

# Add raw counts and within-project percentages above each bar
for container, left_value in zip(ax.containers, [0, 1]):
    for bar, project_count in zip(container, project_order):

        count = project_counts.loc[project_count, left_value]
        percentage = project_percentages.loc[
            project_count,
            left_value
        ]

        ax.annotate(
            f"{count:,}\n({percentage:.1f}%)",
            xy=(
                bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2,
                bar.get_height()
            ),
            xytext=(0, 4),
            textcoords="offset points",
            ha="center",
            va="bottom",
            fontsize=9
        )

ax.set_title(
    "Employee Project Count by Turnover Status",
    fontsize=15,
    pad=15
)

ax.set_xlabel("Number of Projects")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of Employees")

# Replace numeric turnover labels with readable labels
handles, labels = ax.get_legend_handles_labels()

ax.legend(
    handles,
    ["Stayed", "Left"],
    title="Turnover Status"
)

ax.grid(
    axis="y",
    linestyle="--",
    alpha=0.25
)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Interpretation checkpoint — Question 2.3¶

  • At which project counts is turnover most visible?
  • Does the pattern suggest under-allocation, over-allocation, or both?
  • Would percentages reveal anything that raw counts hide?

Write the inference here:

Employee turnover is most visible at both the lowest and highest project counts, supporting patterns of both under-allocation and over-allocation. Employees assigned two projects produced the largest raw number of departures, with 1,567 employees leaving and a turnover rate of 65.6%. At the opposite end, all 256 employees assigned seven projects left, producing the highest turnover rate of 100%. Employees assigned six projects also experienced a high turnover rate of 55.8%, while turnover was substantially lower among employees assigned three or four projects. These results confirm the two turnover profiles identified earlier: employees with very few projects may be underutilized or disengaged, while employees with six or seven projects may be experiencing excessive workload. These explanations remain hypotheses because the project-count plot shows association rather than the reasons employees left.

3.2 Perform K-Means Clustering of Employees Who Left Into Three Clusters¶

Deliverable: a three-cluster K-means result and a scatter plot of satisfaction versus evaluation, colored by cluster. Marking centroids is recommended.

Reproducibility: set a documented random_state.

In [11]:
# TODO 3.2: Fit KMeans with n_clusters=3 and visualize the assigned clusters.
# Sanity checks: cluster counts, centroid coordinates, and stable results with a fixed random state.

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

# Create a K-means model containing three employee clusters
kmeans_model = KMeans(
    n_clusters=3,
    random_state=123,
    n_init=10
)

# Fit the model and assign each departing employee to a cluster
employees_left["cluster"] = kmeans_model.fit_predict(
    clustering_features
)

# Store the cluster centroids
cluster_centroids = pd.DataFrame(
    kmeans_model.cluster_centers_,
    columns=[
        "satisfaction_level",
        "last_evaluation"
    ]
)

cluster_centroids.index.name = "cluster"

# Summarize the three clusters
cluster_summary = employees_left.groupby(
    "cluster"
).agg(
    employee_count=("cluster", "size"),
    mean_satisfaction=("satisfaction_level", "mean"),
    mean_evaluation=("last_evaluation", "mean")
).round(3)

print("Cluster summary:")
display(cluster_summary)

print("Cluster centroids:")
display(cluster_centroids.round(3))

# Define consistent colors for the three clusters
cluster_palette = {
    0: "#D62728",
    1: "#1F77B4",
    2: "#2CA02C"
}

# Plot the employee clusters
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 7))

ax = sns.scatterplot(
    data=employees_left,
    x="satisfaction_level",
    y="last_evaluation",
    hue="cluster",
    palette=cluster_palette,
    alpha=0.55,
    s=55
)

# Plot the centroid of each cluster
plt.scatter(
    cluster_centroids["satisfaction_level"],
    cluster_centroids["last_evaluation"],
    marker="X",
    s=300,
    c=[
        cluster_palette[0],
        cluster_palette[1],
        cluster_palette[2]
    ],
    edgecolor="black",
    linewidth=1.5,
    label="Centroids"
)

# Label each centroid
for cluster_number, centroid in cluster_centroids.iterrows():
    plt.annotate(
        f"Cluster {cluster_number}",
        xy=(
            centroid["satisfaction_level"],
            centroid["last_evaluation"]
        ),
        xytext=(8, 8),
        textcoords="offset points",
        fontsize=10,
        fontweight="bold"
    )

plt.title(
    "K-Means Clusters of Employees Who Left",
    fontsize=15,
    pad=15

3.3 Explain the Employee Clusters¶

Summarize each cluster using its centroid, size, and visible position in the plot. Use descriptive labels only after examining the results.

K-means clustering identified three distinct profiles among the 3,571 employees who left the company. Cluster 0 contained 944 employees, or approximately 26.4% of departing employees. Its centroid showed very low average satisfaction of 0.111 and high average evaluation of 0.869. This group represents highly evaluated but deeply dissatisfied employees. Their departure may be associated with inadequate recognition, limited advancement, compensation concerns, excessive workload, or other unmet expectations.

Cluster 1 was the largest group, containing 1,650 employees, or approximately 46.2% of departing employees. These employees had moderate-to-low average satisfaction of 0.410 and a comparatively low average evaluation of 0.517. This profile may represent employees experiencing poor job fit, insufficient support or training, disengagement, or performance difficulties.

Cluster 2 contained 977 employees, or approximately 27.4% of departing employees. Its members had high average satisfaction of 0.809 and high average evaluation of 0.912. This cluster demonstrates that employees may leave even when they appear satisfied and perform well. Their departures may be influenced by workload, compensation, advancement opportunities, competing job offers, or factors not represented in the dataset.

Overall, the clustering analysis confirms that employees who leave do not form one uniform group. Instead, turnover includes highly evaluated but dissatisfied employees, lower-evaluated employees with moderate-to-low satisfaction, and highly satisfied high performers. Consequently, a single retention strategy may not be appropriate for every employee profile. The proposed explanations remain hypotheses because K-means identifies groups based only on satisfaction and evaluation; it does not determine why the employees left or estimate their probability of leaving.

4. Handle Class Imbalance Using SMOTE

The positive class (left == 1) is the minority class. Preserve an untouched test set and apply SMOTE only to training data.

4.1 Convert Categorical Columns to Numerical Columns¶

The problem statement requires:

  1. Separating categorical and numerical variables.
  2. Applying get_dummies() to categorical variables.
  3. Combining the categorical and numerical variables.

Deliverable: feature matrix X, target vector y, encoded shape, and a list of the created dummy columns.

In [12]:
# TODO 4.1: Separate X and y, identify categorical columns, encode them, and recombine features.
# Checkpoint: left must not remain inside X.
# Checkpoint: all final feature columns should be numerical.

# Define the target column
target_column = "left"

# Separate the target from the predictor variables
y = df[target_column].copy()

predictor_df = df.drop(
    columns=[target_column]
).copy()

# Separate categorical and numerical predictor variables
categorical_features = predictor_df.select_dtypes(
    include=["object", "category"]
).copy()

numerical_features = predictor_df.select_dtypes(
    exclude=["object", "category"]
).copy()

# Display the separated feature groups
print(
    "Categorical feature columns:",
    categorical_features.columns.tolist()
)

print(
    "Numerical feature columns:",
    numerical_features.columns.tolist()
)

# Convert categorical variables into numerical dummy variables
categorical_encoded = pd.get_dummies(
    categorical_features,
    dtype=int
)

# Combine the numerical and encoded categorical features
X = pd.concat(
    [
        numerical_features,
        categorical_encoded
    ],
    axis=1
)

# Ensure the target is stored as integers
y = y.astype(int)

# Display the final results
print("\nOriginal dataset shape:", df.shape)
print("Encoded categorical shape:", categorical_encoded.shape)
print("Feature matrix X shape:", X.shape)
print("Target vector y shape:", y.shape)

print("\nFinal feature columns:")
print(X.columns.tolist())

print("\nTarget distribution:")
print(y.value_counts().sort_index())

# Verify that every feature is now numerical
print("\nFeature data types:")
print(X.dtypes.value_counts())

print("\nFeature matrix preview:")
display(X.head())

print("\nTarget vector preview:")
display(y.head())

4.3 Upsample the Training Dataset Using SMOTE¶

Import SMOTE from the imblearn package and resample the training data only.

Deliverable: class counts before and after SMOTE.

Leakage guard: never apply SMOTE to the full dataset or to the test set. For cross-validation, the most defensible design places SMOTE inside an imblearn pipeline so synthetic examples are created separately within each training fold.

In [14]:
# TODO 4.3: Apply SMOTE to X_train and y_train only.
# Compare y_train.value_counts() before resampling with the resampled class counts.

from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE

# Record the training class counts before SMOTE
class_counts_before = (
    y_train.value_counts()
    .sort_index()
)

# Create and apply SMOTE to the training data only
smote = SMOTE(
    sampling_strategy="auto",
    random_state=123
)

X_train_smote, y_train_smote = smote.fit_resample(
    X_train,
    y_train
)

# Record the class counts after SMOTE
class_counts_after = (
    y_train_smote.value_counts()
    .sort_index()
)

# Compare the class distributions
smote_comparison = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Before SMOTE Count": class_counts_before,
        "Before SMOTE (%)": (
            class_counts_before / class_counts_before.sum() * 100
        ),
        "After SMOTE Count": class_counts_after,
        "After SMOTE (%)": (
            class_counts_after / class_counts_after.sum() * 100
        )
    }
)

# Replace the numerical index with readable class labels
smote_comparison.index = [
    "Stayed (0)",
    "Left (1)"
]

# Display shapes and class distribution
print("Training feature shape before SMOTE:", X_train.shape)
print("Training target shape before SMOTE:", y_train.shape)

print("\nTraining feature shape after SMOTE:", X_train_smote.shape)
print("Training target shape after SMOTE:", y_train_smote.shape)

print("\nClass distribution before and after SMOTE:")
display(smote_comparison.round(2))

5. Perform 5-Fold Cross-Validation Model Training and Evaluation

Use the same folds and evaluation logic for all three candidate models so the comparison is fair. Keep the held-out test set separate from model selection.

Suggested evidence for each model: five-fold scores, mean and standard deviation, holdout predictions, and a classification report.

5.1 Train and Evaluate a Logistic Regression Model¶

Apply five-fold cross-validation and produce the classification report.

Checkpoint: if optimization does not converge, investigate feature scaling or the iteration limit rather than ignoring the warning.

In [15]:
# TODO 5.1: Define, cross-validate, fit, and evaluate Logistic Regression.
# Store the fitted model, predictions, probabilities, CV results, and classification report for Section 6.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import (
    StratifiedKFold,
    cross_validate
)
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE
from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline


# Create a pipeline that scales the features, applies SMOTE,
# and trains the Logistic Regression model
logistic_pipeline = Pipeline(
    steps=[
        (
            "scaler",
            StandardScaler()
        ),
        (
            "smote",
            SMOTE(
                random_state=123
            )
        ),
        (
            "model",
            LogisticRegression(
                max_iter=1000,
                solver="liblinear",
                random_state=123
            )
        )
    ]
)


# Define reproducible stratified five-fold cross-validation
logistic_cv = StratifiedKFold(
    n_splits=5,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=123
)


# Evaluate several classification metrics during cross-validation
logistic_scoring = {
    "accuracy": "accuracy",
    "precision": "precision",
    "recall": "recall",
    "f1": "f1"
}


logistic_cv_results = cross_validate(
    estimator=logistic_pipeline,
    X=X_train,
    y=y_train,
    cv=logistic_cv,
    scoring=logistic_scoring,
    n_jobs=-1
)


# Store the score from each fold
logistic_cv_scores = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Fold": np.arange(1, 6),
        "Accuracy": logistic_cv_results[
            "test_accuracy"
        ],
        "Precision": logistic_cv_results[
            "test_precision"
        ],
        "Recall": logistic_cv_results[
            "test_recall"
        ],
        "F1 Score": logistic_cv_results[
            "test_f1"
        ]
    }
)


print("Logistic Regression five-fold scores:")
display(
    logistic_cv_scores.round(4)
)


# Calculate the mean and standard deviation across the five folds
metric_columns = [
    "Accuracy",
    "Precision",
    "Recall",
    "F1 Score"
]

logistic_cv_summary = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Mean CV Score": logistic_cv_scores[
            metric_columns
        ].mean(),
        "Standard Deviation": logistic_cv_scores[
            metric_columns
        ].std(ddof=0)
    }
)


print("Logistic Regression cross-validation summary:")
display(
    logistic_cv_summary.round(4)
)


# Fit the complete pipeline using the original training data
# The pipeline applies SMOTE internally
logistic_pipeline.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train
)


# Predict the untouched holdout test data
logistic_predictions = logistic_pipeline.predict(
    X_test
)

logistic_probabilities = logistic_pipeline.predict_proba(
    X_test
)[:, 1]


# Preview the holdout predictions
logistic_prediction_preview = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Actual Class": y_test,
        "Predicted Class": logistic_predictions,
        "Probability of Leaving": logistic_probabilities
    },
    index=y_test.index
)


print("Holdout prediction preview:")
display(
    logistic_prediction_preview.head(10).round(4)
)


# Generate the holdout classification report
print("Logistic Regression classification report:\n")

print(
    classification_report(
        y_test,
        logistic_predictions,
        labels=[0, 1],
        target_names=[
            "Stayed (0)",
            "Left (1)"
        ],
        digits=3,
        zero_division=0
    )
)


# Convert the classification report into a DataFrame
logistic_report = classification_report(
    y_test,
    logistic_predictions,
    labels=[0, 1],
    target_names=[
        "Stayed (0)",
        "Left (1)"
    ],
    output_dict=True,
    zero_division=0
)

logistic_report_df = pd.DataFrame(
    logistic_report
).transpose()


print("Classification report table:")
display(
    logistic_report_df.round(3)
)


# Plot the primary classification-report metrics
logistic_report_plot = logistic_report_df.loc[
    [
        "Stayed (0)",
        "Left (1)"
    ],
    [
        "precision",
        "recall",
        "f1-score"
    ]
]


plt.figure(
    figsize=(8, 4)
)

sns.heatmap(
    logistic_report_plot,
    annot=True,
    fmt=".3f",
    cmap="Blues",
    vmin=0,
    vmax=1,
    linewidths=0.5
)

plt.title(
    "Logistic Regression Classification Report",
    fontsize=14,
    pad=12
)

plt.xlabel(
    "Evaluation Metric"
)

plt.ylabel(
    "Employee Class"
)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5.2 Train and Evaluate a Random Forest Classifier¶

Apply five-fold cross-validation and produce the classification report. Use a fixed random state.

In [16]:
# TODO 5.2: Define, cross-validate, fit, and evaluate Random Forest.
# Store outputs under clear Random Forest names so they cannot overwrite the Logistic Regression results.

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import (
    StratifiedKFold,
    cross_validate
)
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE
from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline


# Create the Random Forest pipeline
#
# Random Forest does not require scaling, but SMOTE uses
# distances to locate neighboring observations. Scaling
# prevents large-range features from dominating those distances.
random_forest_pipeline = Pipeline(
    steps=[
        (
            "scaler",
            StandardScaler()
        ),
        (
            "smote",
            SMOTE(
                random_state=123
            )
        ),
        (
            "model",
            RandomForestClassifier(
                n_estimators=100,
                random_state=123
            )
        )
    ]
)


# Define reproducible stratified five-fold cross-validation
random_forest_cv = StratifiedKFold(
    n_splits=5,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=123
)


# Define the evaluation metrics
random_forest_scoring = {
    "accuracy": "accuracy",
    "precision": "precision",
    "recall": "recall",
    "f1": "f1"
}


# Perform five-fold cross-validation using the original
# training data. SMOTE is applied separately within each fold.
random_forest_cv_results = cross_validate(
    estimator=random_forest_pipeline,
    X=X_train,
    y=y_train,
    cv=random_forest_cv,
    scoring=random_forest_scoring,
    n_jobs=-1
)


# Store the evaluation score from each fold
random_forest_cv_scores = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Fold": np.arange(1, 6),
        "Accuracy": random_forest_cv_results[
            "test_accuracy"
        ],
        "Precision": random_forest_cv_results[
            "test_precision"
        ],
        "Recall": random_forest_cv_results[
            "test_recall"
        ],
        "F1 Score": random_forest_cv_results[
            "test_f1"
        ]
    }
)


print("Random Forest five-fold scores:")

display(
    random_forest_cv_scores.round(4)
)


# Calculate the mean and standard deviation across the folds
random_forest_metric_columns = [
    "Accuracy",
    "Precision",
    "Recall",
    "F1 Score"
]


random_forest_cv_summary = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Mean CV Score": random_forest_cv_scores[
            random_forest_metric_columns
        ].mean(),

        "Standard Deviation": random_forest_cv_scores[
            random_forest_metric_columns
        ].std(ddof=0)
    }
)


print("Random Forest cross-validation summary:")

display(
    random_forest_cv_summary.round(4)
)


# Fit the complete pipeline using the original training data
# The pipeline applies scaling and SMOTE internally.
random_forest_pipeline.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train
)


# Predict the classes of the untouched holdout test data
random_forest_predictions = random_forest_pipeline.predict(
    X_test
)


# Store the probability that each employee belongs
# to the turnover class, left = 1
random_forest_probabilities = (
    random_forest_pipeline.predict_proba(
        X_test
    )[:, 1]
)


# Preview the holdout predictions and probabilities
random_forest_prediction_preview = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Actual Class": y_test,
        "Predicted Class": random_forest_predictions,
        "Probability of Leaving": random_forest_probabilities
    },
    index=y_test.index
)


print("Random Forest holdout prediction preview:")

display(
    random_forest_prediction_preview.head(10).round(4)
)


# Print the classification report

print(
    classification_report(
        y_test,

            "Stayed (0)",

        ],

)


# Store the classification report as a DataFrame

5.3 Train and Evaluate a Gradient Boosting Classifier¶

Apply five-fold cross-validation and produce the classification report. Use a fixed random state when supported.

In [17]:
# TODO 5.3: Define, cross-validate, fit, and evaluate Gradient Boosting.
# Store outputs under clear Gradient Boosting names for the Section 6 comparison.

from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import (
    StratifiedKFold,
    cross_validate
)
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE
from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline


# Create the Gradient Boosting pipeline
#
# Gradient Boosting itself does not require scaling.
# StandardScaler is included because SMOTE uses distances
# to identify neighboring minority-class observations.
gradient_boosting_pipeline = Pipeline(
    steps=[
        (
            "scaler",
            StandardScaler()
        ),
        (
            "smote",
            SMOTE(
                random_state=123
            )
        ),
        (
            "model",
            GradientBoostingClassifier(
                n_estimators=100,
                learning_rate=0.1,
                max_depth=3,
                random_state=123
            )
        )
    ]
)


# Define reproducible stratified five-fold cross-validation
gradient_boosting_cv = StratifiedKFold(
    n_splits=5,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=123
)


# Define the evaluation metrics
gradient_boosting_scoring = {
    "accuracy": "accuracy",
    "precision": "precision",
    "recall": "recall",
    "f1": "f1"
}


# Perform five-fold cross-validation using the original
# training data. SMOTE is applied separately within each fold.
gradient_boosting_cv_results = cross_validate(
    estimator=gradient_boosting_pipeline,
    X=X_train,
    y=y_train,
    cv=gradient_boosting_cv,
    scoring=gradient_boosting_scoring,
    n_jobs=-1
)


# Store the evaluation score from each fold
gradient_boosting_cv_scores = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Fold": np.arange(1, 6),
        "Accuracy": gradient_boosting_cv_results[

        ],

        ],
        "Recall": gradient_boosting_cv_results[

        ],

        ]
    }
)

    gradient_boosting_cv_scores.round(4)

# Calculate the mean and standard deviation across the folds

6. Identify the Best Model and Justify the Evaluation Metrics

Select the best model using consistent evidence rather than accuracy alone. Employee turnover is imbalanced, so emphasize performance on employees who actually leave.

Interpretation checkpoint — Question 6.1¶

  • Which model has the highest AUC?
  • Are the differences practically meaningful?
  • Does the ROC comparison agree with the classification reports?

Write the inference here:

The Random Forest achieved the highest ROC-AUC score, indicating the strongest overall ability to distinguish between employees who stayed and those who left. However, its advantage over Gradient Boosting was small and is not practically meaningful, as both models demonstrated excellent discrimination. In contrast, both ensemble models substantially outperformed Logistic Regression. The ROC-AUC comparison agrees with the classification reports: Random Forest performed best overall, Gradient Boosting was a close second, and Logistic Regression was clearly the weakest model. This agreement is based on the models’ relative ranking, not on the numerical closeness of AUC and accuracy, because those metrics measure different aspects of performance.

6.3 Explain Which Confusion-Matrix Metric Should Be Used: Recall or Precision¶

Frame the decision using business costs:

  • False negative: an employee likely to leave is classified as staying.
  • False positive: an employee likely to stay is classified as leaving.

Answer these questions before choosing the primary metric:

  1. Which error is more harmful to Portobello Tech?
  2. What resources are spent when HR acts on a false alarm?
  3. Should one metric be primary while the other remains a guardrail?

Metric justification:

A false negative is likely the more harmful error for Portobello Tech because it represents an employee who is predicted to stay but actually leaves. Missing an at-risk employee prevents HR from intervening and may result in lost productivity, replacement and training costs, redistribution of work, increased hours for remaining employees, and potentially additional turnover caused by the increased workload.

A false positive also creates business costs. If an employee who would have stayed is incorrectly identified as likely to leave, HR may unnecessarily spend time and resources on meetings, stay interviews, retention bonuses, promotions, compensation adjustments, or workload changes. These resources could instead have been directed toward employees who were genuinely at risk.

Therefore, recall for the “Left (1)” class should be the primary metric because maximizing recall reduces the number of actual leavers who are missed. Precision should remain an important guardrail to ensure that HR’s at-risk employee list does not contain too many false alarms. Random Forest provides the strongest balance for this purpose, achieving 0.979 recall and 0.986 precision for employees who left.

Best-model decision¶

Evidence Logistic Regression Random Forest Gradient Boosting
ROC/AUC 0.827 0.995 0.986
Recall for left = 1 0.810 0.979 0.934
Precision for left = 1 0.505 0.986 0.929
F1-score for left = 1 0.622 0.982 0.932
False negatives 136 15 47
CV stability (accuracy SD) 0.0066 0.0010 0.0012

Selected model: Random Forest

Why it is the best fit for this business problem: Random Forest is the best model because it provides the strongest and most consistent performance across all relevant evaluation evidence. It achieved the highest ROC-AUC, recall, precision, and F1-score for employees who left. Most importantly, it produced only 15 false negatives, compared with 47 for Gradient Boosting and 136 for Logistic Regression. Because a false negative represents an employee who is predicted to stay but actually leaves, minimizing these errors directly supports Portobello Tech’s need to identify at-risk employees before turnover occurs. Random Forest also had the lowest cross-validation variability, indicating that its strong performance was consistent across the five folds. Therefore, Random Forest offers the best combination of turnover detection, limited false alarms, and model stability for this business problem.

7. Suggest Retention Strategies for Targeted Employees

Convert the best model's probability estimates into practical risk zones. Retention actions should match the employee's risk level and the patterns discovered in EDA and clustering.

7.1 Use the Best Model to Predict Employee-Turnover Probability in the Test Data¶

Deliverable: one positive-class turnover probability for every row in the untouched test set. Preserve the test indices so probabilities can be joined back to the employee features.

7.2 Categorize Employees Into Four Risk Zones and Recommend Retention Strategies¶

Use non-overlapping boundaries so every probability belongs to exactly one zone:

Risk zone Probability rule Suggested response level
Safe Zone (Green) score < 20% Maintain engagement and monitor periodically
Low-Risk Zone (Yellow) 20% ≤ score < 60% Light-touch check-ins and development support
Medium-Risk Zone (Orange) 60% ≤ score < 90% Manager review and targeted retention plan
High-Risk Zone (Red) score ≥ 90% Immediate, individualized HR intervention

The original problem statement leaves the exact 20%, 60%, and 90% boundary values ambiguous. The rules above close those gaps explicitly.

    employee_percentage = zone_values.loc[
        zone,
        "Percentage_of_Test_Set"
    ]
    
    mean_probability = zone_values.loc[
        zone,
        "Mean_Turnover_Probability"
    ]
    
    return (
        f"{employee_count:,} employees "
        f"({employee_percentage:.1%} of the test set), "
        f"with a mean predicted risk of "
        f"{mean_probability:.1%}. "
        f"{analysis_evidence}"
    )


# Create the completed retention-strategy checkpoint

Final Conclusions and Submission Check

Executive summary¶

Complete this section after the analysis in four short parts:

  1. Turnover profile: the most important patterns found in EDA.
  2. Employee segments: what the three clusters reveal.
  3. Best model: the selected model and the metrics supporting it.
  4. Business action: the most important targeted retention recommendations.

1. Turnover Profile¶

Employee turnover was concentrated at both workload extremes. Employees with only two projects had a 65.6% turnover rate, while those with six or seven projects also experienced very high turnover. The EDA suggests two broad profiles: potentially underutilized or disengaged employees with lower workloads, and highly evaluated employees working excessive hours who may be at risk of burnout. These patterns show associations rather than proven causes.

2. Employee Segments¶

K-means clustering identified three distinct groups among employees who left: 944 highly evaluated but deeply dissatisfied employees, 1,650 employees with moderate-to-low satisfaction and lower evaluations, and 977 satisfied, high-performing employees. These segments demonstrate that turnover does not have a single profile and that retention efforts should be tailored to employees’ different circumstances.

3. Best Model¶

Random Forest was selected as the best model because it produced the strongest and most consistent turnover predictions. It achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.995, recall of 0.979, precision of 0.986, and an F1-score of 0.982 for employees who left. It also produced only 15 false negatives and had the lowest cross-validation variability. This is especially important because a false negative represents an employee whom the company expects to stay but who actually leaves, preventing HR from intervening before the departure.

4. Business Action¶

Portobello Tech should use the model’s risk scores to prioritize retention efforts rather than applying the same intervention to every employee. Green-zone employees should receive normal engagement and periodic monitoring, while Yellow-zone employees should receive light manager check-ins and development support. Orange-zone employees require targeted reviews of workload, job fit, training, recognition, and advancement opportunities. Red-zone employees should receive immediate, individualized HR attention through stay interviews and reviews of workload, career path, recognition, schedule flexibility, promotion eligibility, and compensation. These actions should be matched to each employee’s observed profile because the model identifies turnover risk but does not prove which intervention will cause an employee to stay.

Side Note:¶

The dataset contains 3,008 exact matching rows. Because no unique employee identifier or timestamp is available, it is impossible to determine whether these are accidental duplicate records or distinct employees with identical recorded characteristics. Removing them could discard legitimate employee observations; therefore, they were retained for both exploratory analysis and modeling. This uncertainty remains a limitation when interpreting model performance.

Final notebook checklist¶

  • Every numbered requirement from 1 through 7.2 has been answered.
  • Every plot has a title, labeled axes, readable legend, and written inference.
  • Missing values, duplicates, data types, and ranges were checked.
  • The train-test split is 80:20, stratified, and uses random_state=123.
  • SMOTE was applied only to training data and leakage was avoided during CV.
  • All models were compared using the same folds and evaluation process.
  • ROC/AUC uses probabilities rather than class predictions.
  • Confusion-matrix axes and class labels are explicit.
  • The best-model decision is tied to turnover-class performance and business cost.
  • Risk-zone boundaries cover every score without gaps or overlap.
  • Retention strategies are supported by observed evidence.
  • Kernel restarted and Run All completes from top to bottom without errors.
